Subject: Redwood sizing — OrbitX pilot (initial traffic snapshot)

Hi Marissa,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — the team liked the latency demos. We are starting to scope a small pilot (north-america only) and want Redwood to propose a capacity architecture we can start with. I attached a small CSV with 30 days of token-level request logs (orbitx-current-traffic.csv). High-level notes: 

- User-facing chat product: mix of short prompts (10-40 tokens) and longer context windows for support threads (prompts up to 1.2k tokens; typical response 200-800 tokens).
- Average QPS observed: 8 sustained, with 95th percentile short spikes up to 60 QPS for 3–7 minute windows.
- Session model: conversational session affinity — many requests reuse KV cache; about 35% of requests are continuations within 30s.
- Peak concurrent open sessions: ~1,200 during business hours.

Primary asks: can you provide a recommended starting GPU fleet (SKU mix + recommended reservation sizing and a burst policy) and an estimate for p50/p95 latencies for the given workload using 8k-context LLM variants? Also want a checklist of data we might need for a more precise dedicated sizing.

Happy to jump on a short call if helpful.

Thanks —
Priya Rao
Head of Platform, OrbitX

Hi Priya —

Appreciate the data, this is a great start. Quick clarifying questions that will help scoping a pragmatic starting point:

1) Prompt/response mix: can you share the approximate % split between (a) short Q&A (<=100 tokens total), (b) multi-turn support threads (~500–1,000 tokens), and (c) long context generation (>2k tokens)? If you don't have exact numbers, rough percentages are fine.

2) Model choices: are you set on a single 8k-context variant for the pilot, or are you open to a small family (e.g., 4k quantized variant for high-throughput paths and 8k for heavy contexts)?

3) SLO targets: what's your p50/p95 target for end-to-end generation latency (user-perceived; excludes frontend)?

4) KV-cache reuse cadence: do you have any TTLs or session retention expectations beyond the 30s you mentioned?

I've attached a short probe doc (pre-sales-fleet-probe.docx) with fields we usually use to produce a first-pass reserved capacity recommendation — if you can fill the highlighted cells it will speed things up.

Ben, looping you in for pricing/committed reserve guidance; Priya — we can put together a back-of-envelope fleet mix and follow up with a quick architecture call.

Best,

Marissa / Ben —

Thanks for the context. I dug into the sample CSV and ran a quick back-of-envelope sizing. Notes and recommended starting footprint below (aimed at a predictable monthly reserved commit with a small burst pool):

Summary recommendation (pilot):
- Primary reserved pool: 4 x H100-class instances (or equivalent A100-80 mixes) configured for 8k-context model variants. This gives sustained throughput covering ~80–90% of typical 8 QPS steady-state with KV caching accounted for.
- Burst pool (shared preemptible): 2 x A100-40 equivalents to handle short 60 QPS spikes for 3–7 minute windows. Use autoscale policy with token-based alerter and graceful fallback to a 4k quantized variant when burst capacity is exhausted.
- Expected latency (approx, end-to-end generation only): p50 ~ 120–180 ms; p95 ~ 550–900 ms for 8k-context variants on H100-class with our optimized kernels. On quantized 4k-path p95 drops to ~300–450 ms. These numbers assume continuous batching and ~35% KV hit-rate.

Sizing rationale / assumptions:
- Average request token-workload estimated at ~420 tokens (prompt+response) after accounting for cache reuse.
- Peak simultaneous generation concurrency target derived from 60 QPS spikes and avg token-work ~420 => short-term token-per-second demand implies temporary scaling requirement; burst pool handles this to avoid heavy reserved overcommit.
- We assume model parallel and multi-instance batching efficiencies typical of our serving runtime; real-world p95 will vary with request length variance and tail batching behavior.

Operational suggestions:
- Start with reservation for 4 reserve instances + 2 burst instances; monitor token-per-second and adjust month-to-month.
- Configure a canary route: 80% traffic to primary reserved, 20% to hosted fallback during business hours for additional headroom and graceful degradation.
- Enable KV cache TTL of 5 minutes for sessions that show >2 requests in 30s to improve reuse; this should reduce steady-state unit cost.
- Quantization profile: enable int8 for high-throughput path (4k), keep 8k at full precision for quality-sensitive flows.

Next steps we can take for a tighter estimate (what to ask the customer):
- More precise prompt/response percentile distributions (p10/p50/p90 for token lengths).
- Token emission rates per request (or average generation length) broken down by path and session.
- A sample of 1–2 hours of real-time traffic (not aggregated) to test tail behavior and short spike characteristics.

I attached my rough notes (rough-sizing-notes.pdf). If you want, I can turn this into a slide for the pilot SOW and map it to a monthly committed cost estimate.

Cheers,
Dev Patel
